extracted.intended_audience: scholars and policymakers studying regulatory impact analysis, science use in policymaking, and administrative rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and analyzing how much scientific research agencies invoke in Regulatory Impact Analyses (RIAs) for economically significant US federal rules, and testing whether political attention (public comments, OIRA meetings, media coverage) predicts greater science use. Includes data definitions, sources, coding rules, and statistical modeling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable — scientific citation count in an RIA
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of scientific citations in an RIA is the dependent variable. A citation was coded as “scientific” if it is published in a scholarly journal in the Institute for the Scientific Information’s Web of Science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution is heavily skewed (range 0–258, median 3, mean 12.2; total 1,234 citations across 101 RIAs). The authors note this is a measure of volume of science invoked, not of regulatory quality; prior work shows cited articles tend to come from higher-impact journals. Use citation count to study change in volume of science, acknowledging possible instrumental/window-dressing uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of public attention — post-filtering number of public comments (regulations.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the post-filtering number of public comments directed to each RIA’s docket on regulations.gov as the measure of general public attention to a proposed regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments include those submitted directly to regs.gov or to the agency; agencies filter comments before posting (reasons include private/proprietary info, inappropriate language, duplicate mass-mail campaigns). Posting delays occur. The authors use post-filtered counts to partly address astroturfing concerns; one RIA lacking a docket page was omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of elite attention — number of OIRA meetings requested (OIRA/CPR records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the number of meetings requested with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) concerning the proposed rule as an indicator of attention from organized/elite interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting records sourced from CPR’s collection and OIRA’s database, matched to RIAs by Regulatory Identification Number (RIN). Meetings are temporally restricted to those occurring before the RIA release date. Meetings range 0–47 (mean 1.46, median 0). Meetings are taken to represent organized interests (often business/trade associations); additional analysis found no significant correlation between meeting participant type and citation counts, suggesting the effect is driven by number of meetings rather than participant type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of media attention — Washington Post articles about issuing agency (90 days prior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure media attention as the number of Washington Post articles about the executive agency that issued the regulation in the 90 days before the RIA’s release date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate/similar articles (high similarity by LexisNexis) are excluded to capture unique pieces. Articles measure agency-level attention (not necessarily the specific regulation); authors justify agency-level media attention as a signal of rising salience and potential to influence regulators. This variable is temporal (90-day window) and precedes RIA release to support causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case selection — economically significant RIAs ($100 million+), 2008–2012
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze all RIAs produced for economically significant proposed rules (those estimated to have an economic impact of $100 million or more) from 2008–2012, totaling 101 documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economically significant designation is made by OIRA per Executive Order 12291; agencies must submit RIAs to OIRA for review and approval for such rules. RIAs are drawn from the Mercatus Center collection; RIAs span 13 agencies with varying counts (e.g., EPA 25, DOT 15, DOL 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of agency scientific integrity policy (0–3 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for agency-level science policies by coding agency scientific integrity on a scale from 0 to 3 based on the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) comparative analysis: 3 = actively promote and support scientific integrity; 2 = need additional work; 1 = do not make adequate commitments; 0 = absence of a policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding applied to the closest legislative office (e.g., HHS coded at department level with FDA/CDC coded separately where appropriate). This categorical control captures communications, personnel, issue area, culture, SOPs, and other agency characteristics. The authors find higher-rated integrity policies strongly related to greater citation counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal rule for independent variables — include only measures before RIA release
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include public comments, OIRA meetings, and media coverage that occur before the release date of the RIA so that political attention temporally precedes the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temporal restriction supports inference that attention drives agency use of science (not vice versa). Meetings from CPR/OIRA and media/article counts were measured with this temporal constraint; comments posting delays are noted as a caveat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and matching procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple administrative and bibliometric sources and match across them (Mercatus Center RIAs; citation data from Desmarais & Hird 2013; regulations.gov for comments; CPR/OIRA meeting records matched via RIN; LexisNexis for Washington Post articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research assistants crosschecked CPR meeting data for accuracy and collected additional meeting records through December 2012. RIN is used to match RIAs to OIRA meeting records. Matching and source limitations (e.g., one missing docket) are documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choices for count data — quasi-Poisson with log-transformed predictors and optional page-length offset
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate effects using quasi-Poisson regression to account for overdispersion in the count-dependent variable; take the natural log of each independent variable (plus one) to model decreasing marginal effects; optionally include log(page length) as an offset to model citation rate per page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasi-Poisson chosen to address overdispersion and small-sample convergence issues. Including page-length offset scales expected citation counts by document length (modeled as events per page). Models also examine within-agency subsamples (e.g., EPA-only) to test robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caveat — citation volume ≠ regulatory quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly note that the study does not assess whether more science in an RIA indicates a higher-quality regulation; the focus is on whether political attention alters the volume of science invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors discuss that citations can bolster pre-existing claims or meaningfully supplement justifications; while cited articles tend to have higher impact factors, citation count alone does not measure influence or quality of the final rule. Future work suggested to analyze content/quality thresholds and comment content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling skewness and nonlinearity (log transforms and marginal effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because citation counts are heavily skewed and exhibit a heavy right tail, independent variables are log-transformed (plus one) and model predictions are interpreted substantively using predicted values and marginal effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors present figures of distributions and predicted citation counts (e.g., each additional OIRA meeting ≈ one additional predicted cite; a one SD increase in comments ≈ ~50% increase in predicted citations). Collinearity between predictors (e.g., when adding news coverage) is noted in subgroup models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-agency controls and subgroup analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for baseline within-agency consistency in science use by including a categorical agency variable and conducting within-agency analyses (e.g., EPA-only models) to test whether attention effects hold inside agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding that public comments and OIRA meetings remain positive predictors within EPA (though news coverage can reduce comment significance due to collinearity) supports interpretation that agencies change behavior conditional on external attention, not just agency-level differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions and limitations of attention sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and distinguish three origins of political attentiveness: general public (public comments), elite policy actors (OIRA meetings), and media (news coverage), with discussion of their accessibility and representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comments are low-cost and broadly accessible but susceptible to mass-mail campaigns; OIRA meetings are less accessible and dominated by narrow interests; media can both depend on and drive public attention and shift agenda attribution. These conceptual distinctions motivate using all three complementary measures to capture political controversy 'writ large.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtering and astroturfing mitigation for comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that regulations.gov filters comments and that posted counts may undercount submissions; use post-filtering numbers to mitigate effects of duplicate/mass-mail campaigns (astroturfing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies filter comments for private/proprietary info, inappropriate language, duplicates; it is impossible to know whether posted comments are individual or coordinated campaigns, but post-filtering counts reduce but do not eliminate astroturfing concerns. Authors note potential lag in posting as a limitation.
